## Unnecessary Re-renders in React ### 1. Reference Equality React re-renders a component when its props change. For primitives, this is value equality (`5 === 5`). For objects and functions, it's **reference equality** — a new object literal `{}` is never `===` to another `{}`, even with identical contents. ```jsx // Every render creates a new object reference → child always re-renders // Every render creates a new function reference → child always re-renders doSomething()} /> ``` React doesn't deep-compare props by default, so any new reference is treated as a changed prop. --- ### 2. React.memo, useMemo, useCallback **`React.memo`** — wraps a component to skip re-rendering if props are shallowly equal. Useless without also stabilizing the props being passed. ```jsx const Child = React.memo(({ value }) =>
{value}
); ``` Use when: a pure component renders often with the same props, and rendering is expensive. **`useCallback`** — memoizes a function reference across renders. ```jsx const handleClick = useCallback(() => doSomething(id), [id]); ``` Use when: passing a callback to a `React.memo` child, or as a dependency of another hook. **`useMemo`** — memoizes a computed value. ```jsx const sorted = useMemo(() => items.sort(compareFn), [items]); ``` Use when: the computation is genuinely expensive, or you need a stable object/array reference to prevent downstream re-renders. **Rule of thumb:** don't reach for these by default. Profile first. Memoization has a cost — wrong dependencies cause stale bugs, and the overhead isn't free. --- ### 3. Context Provider Pitfalls A context value is compared by reference. If you create the value inline on every render, **all consumers re-render on every parent render** regardless of whether the data changed. ```jsx // Bad: new object every render → all consumers re-render ``` ```jsx // Good: stable reference unless user/setUser actually changes const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user, setUser]); ``` A deeper fix: split context into separate providers for data that changes at different rates (e.g., `UserContext` vs. `UserDispatchContext`). Dispatch functions from `useReducer` are stable, so consumers that only need dispatch never re-render when state changes. --- ### 4. Before / After **Before** — `ExpensiveList` re-renders on every keystroke in the parent, even though `items` didn't change: ```jsx function Parent() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(''); const items = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']; return ( <> setQuery(e.target.value)} /> console.log(item)} // new function every render /> ); } const ExpensiveList = ({ items, onSelect }) => { /* heavy render */ }; ``` **After** — stable references mean `ExpensiveList` only re-renders when `items` actually changes: ```jsx const ITEMS = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry']; // stable: defined outside component function Parent() { const [query, setQuery] = useState(''); const handleSelect = useCallback((item) => console.log(item), []); // stable ref return ( <> setQuery(e.target.value)} /> ); } const ExpensiveList = React.memo(({ items, onSelect }) => { /* heavy render */ }); ``` Key changes: - `ITEMS` moved outside the component (constant, no memo needed) - `onSelect` wrapped in `useCallback` with empty deps (never changes) - `ExpensiveList` wrapped in `React.memo` to actually use the stable props
